frames.narration: A caller looks for one value in a sorted list of 1,000,000 items. A scan can need 1,000,000 probes. Halving needs 20, because every probe discards half of the range that could still hold the value.

The loop is safe when it keeps one promise: the value, if present, is in the range from lo up to but not including hi. Too small in the middle means lo = mid + 1, otherwise hi = mid. Each branch keeps the promise and shrinks the range.

Break it: write lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1. When lo and hi are neighbours, mid equals lo and the range stops shrinking. In the model this hangs on the last item, the middle item and a missing value, and works on the first item, so a one-target test passes.

Duplicates. With every value stored 4 times in 1,000 items, the textbook loop stops at the first probe that hits and returns index 2 for a value whose first copy is at index 0. Any match is not the first match.
A lower-bound search does not stop at a hit. It keeps moving hi down until the range holds the first position that is not smaller than the target: 11 probes, index 0, every time.

Another trap, in languages with 32-bit integers: (lo + hi) / 2 with lo = 1,500,000,000 and hi = 2,000,000,000 wraps the sum to -794,967,296, so the midpoint is -397,483,648, outside the range. lo + (hi - lo) / 2 gives 1,750,000,000.

Halving also searches an answer space. For the smallest ship capacity that moves 1,000 packages in 3 days there is no array: each capacity is tested by one pass over the packages. 13 checks (13,000 steps) find 3,503, where counting up from 20 would need 3,484 checks.
